paragraphs: AGENT tests whether machine learning systems can reason about the hidden motives behind another agent’s actions. Its focus is intuitive psychology: interpreting behavior in terms of goals, effort, constraints, and rewards. The motivating question is whether systems that predict or explain actions actually capture the principles people use when reasoning about other agents.

The benchmark uses procedurally generated 3D animations organized around four scenarios: preferences between goals, efficient actions, constraints that are not directly visible, and trade-offs between costs and rewards. These scenarios make different aspects of psychological reasoning explicit. Human ratings validate the benchmark, and its evaluation protocol emphasizes generalization rather than success only on familiar situations.

The authors compare systems based on Bayesian inverse planning and a Theory of Mind neural network. Their results suggest that human-level performance on these tests requires learned or built-in representations of planning that combine utility calculations with knowledge of objects and physics. This is an interpretation supported by the benchmark results, rather than a universal proof about every possible reasoning system.
icml-2021-agent-a-benchmark-for-core-psy.tldr: AGENT uses animated scenarios to test whether models understand actions through goals, constraints, efficiency, and rewards.

paragraphs: Learning from several source domains requires deciding which sources are useful for a target task and how to combine them. This paper studies the case where sources have different label distributions. Those differences matter because a source can contain relevant information even when its overall distribution looks unlike the target’s.

The proposed method bases source aggregation mainly on similarity between semantic conditional distributions, rather than similarity between marginal distributions. In plain language, it gives greater importance to relationships conditioned on semantic information than to the overall mixture of observations. This changes the basis for judging relevance when differences in class proportions can make broad distribution comparisons misleading.

The authors also provide one framework for three settings: adaptation with limited target labels, adaptation without target labels, and partial-label unsupervised adaptation. Their experiments report significant improvements over the evaluated baselines. The contribution is therefore both a different criterion for combining sources and a shared approach across several adaptation scenarios; the reported performance advantage is empirical.
icml-2021-aggregating-from-multiple-targ.tldr: The method combines source domains using semantic conditional similarity to handle differences in label distributions.

paragraphs: A backdoored model behaves maliciously when an input contains a particular trigger pattern. One detection strategy searches for small patterns that make otherwise benign inputs receive a chosen target label. The paper addresses the cost of this search: existing optimization-based defenses can require work that grows quadratically with the number of classes.

The proposed K-Arm method borrows the idea of allocating effort among competing options from multi-arm bandits. It repeatedly and stochastically chooses promising labels for further optimization, guided by an objective function. As the search proceeds, it revises those choices. This concentrates computation while reducing uncertainty about which labels deserve attention, supporting both faster scanning and more accurate detection.

The authors evaluate the method on more than 4,000 models from rounds one through four of the IARPA TrojAI competition. They report top leaderboard performance at submission time and better accuracy and scanning time than five compared techniques. These findings support adaptive search as a practical way to scan models with many classes.
icml-2021-backdoor-scanning-for-deep-neu.tldr: K-Arm backdoor scanning adaptively concentrates trigger-search effort on promising labels, improving detection accuracy and scanning time in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how well a target policy would perform using historical data collected by a different behavior policy. The central challenge is that the available observations come from decisions made under another policy. This paper focuses on expressing uncertainty about the resulting value estimate, rather than reporting only a single number.

The proposed procedure constructs a confidence interval for the target policy’s value. Such an interval makes uncertainty part of the evaluation output: the estimated value is accompanied by a range intended to quantify its statistical uncertainty. This distinction matters whenever the usefulness of an evaluation depends on how precisely the available historical data support it.

The authors describe their interval procedure as efficient, robust, and flexible, and support it through theoretical results and numerical experiments. They also provide a Python implementation. The stated contribution is a method for uncertainty quantification in off-policy evaluation, with both mathematical and experimental justification, making confidence intervals a central part of evaluating a policy from previously collected data.
icml-2021-deeply-debiased-off-policy-int.tldr: The paper develops a theoretically and numerically supported procedure for confidence intervals on policy values estimated from historical off-policy data.

paragraphs: Choosing an optimizer means choosing how a neural network updates its parameters during training. With hundreds of proposed methods and limited decisive guidance, that choice often rests on anecdotes. This paper replaces some of that guesswork with a standardized comparison of fifteen popular optimizers, covering more than 50,000 individual runs.

The results show substantial variation across tasks, with no optimizer clearly dominating every tested setting. One useful practical finding is that trying several optimizers with their default settings worked approximately as well as tuning the hyperparameters of one fixed optimizer. In these experiments, exploring the optimizer choice itself was therefore a competitive use of search effort.

The authors identify a smaller collection of optimizer and parameter choices that generally produced competitive results. Adam remains strong: newer methods did not significantly and consistently outperform it. These are evidence-backed heuristics from the tested tasks, not a universal ranking. The released results also provide well-tuned reference points for evaluating new optimization methods without repeating the full benchmark.
icml-2021-descending-through-a-crowded-v.tldr: A large standardized benchmark finds task-dependent optimizer performance, with Adam competitive and default-setting optimizer searches approximately matching single-optimizer tuning.

paragraphs: Message passing networks predict molecular properties by exchanging information between atoms in a graph. Although these networks handle large training sets well, earlier approaches were less data efficient than kernel methods. This paper identifies limitations of rotation-invariant representations as a major contributor and develops a representation that retains directional information.

The resulting polarizable atom interaction neural network, PaiNN, uses rotationally equivariant message passing. Equivariance means that rotating a molecule transforms its internal representations consistently with that rotation, instead of requiring every representation to stay unchanged. This is particularly useful for tensorial properties, whose description depends on spatial direction and must respond appropriately when the molecule rotates.

PaiNN improves performance over previous networks on common molecular benchmarks while reducing model size and inference time. The authors then use its atom-level representations to predict tensorial properties and simulate molecular spectra. For those simulations, they report speedups of four to five orders of magnitude relative to the electronic structure reference, connecting the representation change to a substantial computational benefit.
icml-2021-equivariant-message-passing-fo.tldr: PaiNN uses rotation-equivariant molecular representations to improve benchmark predictions and greatly accelerate the reported molecular spectra simulations.

paragraphs: Spherical data can be represented by dividing the faces of a cube or another Platonic solid into pixels. This creates two interacting kinds of symmetry: transformations of the whole solid and local geometric transformations within each face. The paper argues that treating them as a simple hierarchy does not adequately capture how they interact.

The authors use group theory to describe that interaction and identify linear operations that are equivariant to it. Such operations make network representations transform consistently with the modeled symmetries. They also introduce equivariant padding, so the treatment of boundaries respects the same structure. Together, these components provide building blocks for deep networks on pixelized spheres.

The resulting networks generalize gauge equivariant convolutional networks for this representation of spherical data. They achieve state-of-the-art results on the reported climate semantic segmentation and omnidirectional image processing tasks. The contribution links a more complete treatment of global and local symmetries to concrete network operations, with empirical evidence that those operations are useful for spherical prediction problems.
icml-2021-equivariant-networks-for-pixel.tldr: The paper builds networks for pixelized spheres that respect interacting global and local symmetries, improving results on climate and omnidirectional image tasks.

paragraphs: Feature attribution methods often explain a prediction by comparing an input with a baseline. The baseline choice becomes especially important when the question is why the classifier chose one particular class instead of another. Features shared by both classes may explain the broad category while doing little to explain that specific distinction.

GANMEX uses a generative adversarial network that incorporates the classifier being explained. It selects a baseline as the closest realistic sample belonging to the specified alternative class. This gives the attribution method a comparison tied to the requested contrast, helping it emphasize differentiating features instead of features common to both classes.

The authors report improved saliency maps and stronger results on multiple evaluation metrics compared with existing baselines. They also examine cascading model randomization, addressing the concern that attribution outputs can remain insensitive when the model changes. GANMEX performs better under that evaluation as well. The findings make baseline construction an active part of producing explanations that reflect both the selected alternative class and the classifier.
icml-2021-ganmex-one-vs-one-attributions.tldr: GANMEX generates realistic alternative-class baselines to improve explanations of why a classifier chose one class over another.

paragraphs: Data poisoning and backdoor attacks alter training data so that a model later fails during inference. This paper asks how dangerous existing methods are when evaluated consistently and realistically. Its starting concern is that even attacks pursuing the same objective had been tested under different conditions, making their apparent effectiveness difficult to compare.

The authors apply rigorous testing and find that attack results are highly sensitive to the evaluation setup. They also find that existing methods may fail to generalize to realistic settings. This means that success in one experimental configuration does not, by itself, establish how well an attack will work under another configuration.

The paper develops standardized benchmarks for both poisoning and backdoor attacks to support fairer future comparisons. It treats earlier methods as valuable prototypes while examining how far their demonstrated capabilities extend. The central contribution is therefore a better basis for assessing the threat: consistent evaluation can distinguish strong attack performance from results that depend heavily on particular testing choices.
icml-2021-just-how-toxic-is-data-poisoni.tldr: Standardized testing shows that poisoning and backdoor attack effectiveness depends strongly on evaluation conditions and may not carry over to realistic settings.

paragraphs: Initialization-based meta-learning learns a shared starting point from which models adapt to individual tasks. Extending it to many-shot learning creates a difficulty: task adaptation can require long sequences of gradient updates. The authors first show that allowing more of these inner steps better captures heterogeneous, large-scale task distributions and produces better starting parameters.

Their method addresses the resulting tension between long task-specific training trajectories and frequent updates to the shared initialization. When that initialization changes, they estimate how the task-specific parameters should shift in response. This allows the method to increase the frequency of meta-updates even while working with long inner optimization trajectories.

The paper reports that this approach greatly improves convergence at the meta-learning level and the quality of the learned initializations. Evaluations on heterogeneous large-scale tasks show substantial advantages over previous first-order meta-learning methods in generalization and convergence, as well as over multi-task learning and fine-tuning baselines. The practical contribution is a way to combine deeper task adaptation with more frequent learning of the shared starting point.
icml-2021-large-scale-meta-learning-with.tldr: Continual trajectory shifting enables frequent meta-updates during long task adaptation sequences, improving learned initializations in large-scale experiments.

paragraphs: Molecular conformation generation predicts stable three-dimensional structures from a two-dimensional molecular graph. Existing learning approaches often predict interatomic distances and then construct coordinates that satisfy them. The paper identifies a potential source of additional error in this pipeline: noisy distance predictions can create further errors during coordinate reconstruction.

ConfGF instead learns the gradient of the log probability density over atomic coordinates. This gradient field supplies directions for generating conformations through Langevin dynamics. The field must be equivariant to rotations and translations, so that changing a molecule’s orientation or position changes the predicted directions consistently with its geometry.

The authors show that estimating coordinate gradient fields can be translated into estimating gradient fields over interatomic distances. They use this relationship to develop an algorithm based on score-based generative modeling. Distances therefore help construct the coordinate field rather than serving only as constraints for a separate reconstruction stage. Across multiple evaluated tasks, ConfGF significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art baselines, supporting this route to generating molecular structures.
icml-2021-learning-gradient-fields-for-m.tldr: ConfGF learns geometry-consistent gradient fields to generate molecular conformations directly through Langevin dynamics.

paragraphs: Deep metric learning trains a neural network to place similar examples near one another in a lower-dimensional representation space. Many approaches learn from pairs or triplets of examples. This paper argues that those local comparisons leave broader relationships within a training batch underused, limiting how much of the batch’s structure informs training.

The proposed method connects all examples in a mini-batch through a message passing network. Each example’s representation is refined using messages from the others, allowing training to account for the group as a whole. An attention mechanism assigns different importance to different neighbors, since examples contribute unequally to identifying a useful decision boundary.

The authors report state-of-the-art clustering and image retrieval results on CUB-200-2011, Cars196, Stanford Online Products, and In-Shop Clothes. These findings support using relationships across an entire batch to improve learned representations. The approach expands the information available during training beyond isolated comparisons while allowing the model to emphasize the connections that matter most for distinguishing examples.
icml-2021-learning-intra-batch-connectio.tldr: Attention-weighted message passing across training batches improves metric learning by incorporating relationships beyond pairs and triplets.

paragraphs: GAN training is difficult to monitor because its loss curves do not straightforwardly reveal whether generated data are improving. Duality gap offers a game-theoretic monitoring measure, but its use is restricted to convergence toward a Nash equilibrium. The paper points out that modeling the data distribution does not always require convergence to that kind of equilibrium.

The authors introduce proximal duality gap to cover a more general training setting, including cases where Nash equilibria may not exist. They theoretically show that it can monitor convergence to a broader family of equilibria containing Nash equilibria. This expands the kinds of training outcomes the measure is designed to characterize.

The paper also establishes theoretical relationships between proximal duality gap and the divergence between real and generated distributions for different GAN formulations. That connection gives the monitoring statistic meaning in terms of the modeling objective, beyond its game-theoretic definition. Experiments validate its usefulness for monitoring and influencing training, supporting it as a broader tool for understanding GAN convergence.
icml-2021-on-characterizing-gan-converge.tldr: Proximal duality gap broadens GAN convergence monitoring beyond Nash equilibria and connects it theoretically to distributional mismatch.

paragraphs: This paper studies online active learning of homogeneous halfspaces: linear decision boundaries passing through the origin. The learner selectively requests labels while some labels may be adversarially corrupted. The objective is to reach a target error efficiently, both in labels requested and in examples examined.

The authors give a polynomial-time, Perceptron-like algorithm with near-optimal label complexity. The guarantee assumes an isotropic log-concave input distribution and the stated noise condition ν = Ω(ε), where ε is the target error. Up to suppressed logarithmic factors, label use scales with dimension times polylogarithmic dependence on inverse error, while sample use scales as dimension divided by error.

If the learner additionally knows that the target uses only s attributes, the bounds depend primarily on s, with logarithmic dependence on the ambient dimension. An agnostic corollary removes the noise-rate assumption and gives error O(OPT) + ε, where OPT is the smallest error any homogeneous halfspace can achieve. This provides a comparison to the best available halfspace rather than promising arbitrarily small error under unrestricted noise.
icml-2021-on-the-power-of-localized-perc.tldr: A Perceptron-like active learner achieves near-optimal label complexity for noisy halfspaces under stated distributional and noise conditions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to allocate agents among resources when the benefit of an allocation is initially unknown. Shared mobility provides the motivating application: vehicles must be positioned in useful areas while demand is learned from experience. The aim is to maximize accumulated welfare as decisions and observations arrive over time.

Each resource’s welfare is modeled as a monotone function with diminishing returns, formally a DR-submodular function, and may depend on changing contextual information. The authors turn allocation into a repeated game in which agents learn through regret minimization. They propose two reward designs using upper confidence bounds around the unknown welfare functions, incorporating uncertainty into the incentives agents receive.

The theoretical analysis bounds the gap between the game’s accumulated welfare and the highest welfare attainable in hindsight. A realistic shared-mobility case study then uses observed trip data to learn demand patterns and improve operation. The contribution connects distributed decision-making with uncertainty-aware learning under the stated diminishing-returns model, rather than requiring the allocation benefits to be known beforehand.
icml-2021-online-submodular-resource-all.tldr: A distributed learning game allocates resources under unknown, context-dependent diminishing returns and improves shared-mobility rebalancing in a case study.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning aims to train models collaboratively while allowing different clients to have different data distributions. Sharing information is useful, but each client may need a distinct model. This paper proposes pFedHN, which uses a central hypernetwork to generate an individual model for each participating client.

A hypernetwork produces the parameters of other networks. Here, one shared generator provides a route for information to pass across clients while retaining the ability to create diverse personalized models. Because the hypernetwork’s own parameters are never transmitted, its trainable size is decoupled from communication cost. This makes the architecture’s shared learning capacity distinct from the parameters that must be communicated.

Across several personalized federated learning challenges, pFedHN outperforms the previous methods evaluated by the authors. They also show better generalization to new clients whose distributions differ from those observed during training. These empirical findings suggest that sharing a model-generating mechanism can support both personalization for existing clients and adaptation to previously unseen client distributions.
icml-2021-personalized-federated-learnin.tldr: pFedHN shares a central hypernetwork that generates personalized client models and improves performance on the evaluated federated learning challenges.

paragraphs: Finding a high-value matching means selecting compatible pairs of vertices in a weighted graph. This paper considers a learning version in which the relevant rewards must be discovered through sequential sampling. At each step, the learner samples either a pair or a full matching and receives semi-bandit feedback about the sampled choices.

The key assumption is that the graph’s adjacency matrix has rank one. This imposes a strong shared structure on its entries, allowing observations about some pairs to inform the broader matching problem. The authors prove that exploiting this assumption can improve the sample complexity and regret of existing algorithms.

These two improvements address different objectives: sample complexity concerns how much sampling is needed to learn, while regret measures reward lost during sequential decisions. The paper shows that dependence on the number of vertices can be reduced as far as linear, apart from polylogarithmic factors. The result is conditional on the rank-one structure; it establishes how that structure can make matching problems statistically easier to learn.
icml-2021-pure-exploration-and-regret-mi.tldr: Under a rank-one adjacency assumption, matching bandit algorithms can achieve sample complexity and regret with near-linear dependence on vertex count.

paragraphs: Robots operating in environments without external instrumentation must learn from onboard inputs such as camera images and joint measurements. These observations can be high dimensional and only partially reveal the environment’s state. RRL addresses this policy-learning problem by bringing features from a pretrained ResNet into a standard reinforcement learning pipeline.

The approach uses an existing visual representation as part of learning behavior, connecting advances in representation learning, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning. Its appeal is the simplicity of this combination. The relevant comparison is learning directly from the state, which avoids the difficulty of interpreting visual observations before choosing actions.

In a simulated dexterous manipulation benchmark, RRL learns behaviors involving substantial contact where the compared state-of-the-art methods fail to make significant progress. The authors report performance and sample efficiency comparable to learning from state information, including in complex high-dimensional domains. These findings show that pretrained visual features can be effective within the evaluated control setting, supporting a straightforward route from visual observations to learned behavior.
icml-2021-rrl-resnet-as-representation-f.tldr: RRL combines pretrained ResNet features with reinforcement learning to achieve strong visual control results in simulated dexterous manipulation.

paragraphs: Hybrid trajectories combine smooth evolution with sudden jumps or switches in the governing dynamics. Latent ordinary differential equation models can represent irregularly sampled time series, but are not designed for these interruptions. LatSegODE addresses this by combining smooth latent dynamics with explicit detection of where one segment ends and another begins.

The approach applies when a latent ODE can be trained on the smooth flows between discontinuities. It uses the pruned exact linear time algorithm, PELT, to select changepoints where the latent dynamics restart. The segmentation seeks a high joint probability for the resulting piecewise continuous representation, tying boundary placement to how well the model explains the trajectory.

The authors propose marginal likelihood as PELT’s scoring function, avoiding the need for a model-complexity-based penalty. They report better reconstruction and segmentation than the evaluated baselines on sine-wave data, Lotka–Volterra dynamics, and UCI Character Trajectories. The contribution is a way to preserve smooth modeling within segments while explicitly accommodating discontinuities between them.
icml-2021-segmenting-hybrid-trajectories.tldr: LatSegODE combines latent ODEs with changepoint detection to reconstruct and segment trajectories containing jumps or changing dynamics.

paragraphs: Attention maps show how positions in a sequence attend to one another. Earlier analyses often inspected already pretrained models and used the observed patterns to design sparse attention masks. This paper instead examines the importance of attention positions during pretraining, asking which connections matter while the model is being learned.

The authors find that diagonal attention entries, which connect a position to itself, are the least important compared with other positions. They also provide a proof supporting removal of these entries without deterioration in model performance. This challenges the inference that a connection’s appearance in a trained attention map necessarily establishes its importance during training.

The paper introduces a Differentiable Attention Mask algorithm to guide the design of SparseBERT. Its experiments support the reported findings about attention positions and demonstrate the effect of the masking algorithm. The contribution combines an analysis of attention during pretraining with a method for designing sparse attention, grounding architectural choices in the importance of connections as learning takes place.
icml-2021-sparsebert-rethinking-the-impo.tldr: SparseBERT studies attention importance during pretraining and uses differentiable masks, finding diagonal attention entries least important.

paragraphs: Exploration in reinforcement learning becomes difficult when observations are high dimensional. RE3 encourages broader exploration by using state entropy as an intrinsic reward: the learner receives an internal incentive related to the diversity of states it visits. The challenge is estimating that diversity efficiently from complex observations.

The method maps observations into a lower-dimensional space using a convolutional encoder and applies a nearest-neighbor entropy estimator there. Its distinctive choice is to initialize the encoder randomly and keep it fixed throughout training. The authors find that this provides stable, computationally efficient entropy estimates, so the exploration signal does not require learning and continually updating the encoder.

Experiments show significant improvements in sample efficiency for both model-free and model-based reinforcement learning on locomotion and navigation tasks from DeepMind Control Suite and MiniGrid. RE3 also learns diverse behaviors without external rewards, which improves sample efficiency on downstream tasks. The findings demonstrate that a fixed random representation can be useful for driving exploration in the evaluated environments.
icml-2021-state-entropy-maximization-wit.tldr: RE3 estimates state diversity with a fixed random encoder and uses it as an intrinsic reward to improve exploration efficiency.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates the performance of a target policy using data produced by another policy. Importance sampling adjusts for the difference through likelihood ratios. Its simplicity and unbiasedness make it attractive, but the resulting estimates can have high variance, particularly when the observed trajectories have different lengths.

OSIRIS reduces variance by selectively leaving out likelihood ratios associated with certain states. The organizing idea is state relevance to return: corrections attached to states that are irrelevant in the required sense can introduce variability without being needed for the value estimate. The method therefore changes which parts of a trajectory contribute to the importance weighting.

The authors formalize conditions under which OSIRIS remains unbiased and has lower variance than ordinary importance sampling, and demonstrate these properties empirically. The guarantee depends on those conditions; arbitrary omission is not the stated result. The contribution is a principled way to use state relevance when constructing an estimator, preserving correctness while reducing unnecessary variability where the analysis applies.
icml-2021-state-relevance-for-off-policy.tldr: OSIRIS selectively omits state-level importance ratios to reduce off-policy evaluation variance while retaining unbiasedness under formalized conditions.

paragraphs: An observed difference between groups may reflect a classifier’s behavior or randomness in the audit data. This paper develops statistical tests for deciding whether a classifier fails specified group fairness criteria. The framework accommodates a wide range of fairness notions, including criteria that create difficult discontinuities in model parameters.

The test projects the empirical data distribution onto a set of probability models satisfying the fairness requirements. Optimal transport measures the adjustment needed to reach that set, producing a statistic that can be computed through linear programming. The authors derive its asymptotic distribution explicitly, providing the statistical basis for interpreting the observed distance.

The framework also supports composite fairness hypotheses and multiple sensitive attributes. Its transport formulation adds an interpretable output: the smallest covariate perturbations that would eliminate the bias observed in the audit. This connects the statistical test to concrete changes in the observed inputs, helping explain the discrepancy being detected while keeping the assessment tied to the selected fairness criteria.
icml-2021-testing-group-fairness-via-opt.tldr: Optimal transport projections provide statistical tests of group fairness and characterize the smallest input changes that eliminate observed audit bias.

paragraphs: The paper studies contextual bandits in which a learner chooses several options at once from a potentially enormous collection. It observes all or some rewards for the chosen options and must improve future choices. Advertising and recommendation motivate this setting, where selecting useful candidates must remain computationally feasible.

For the non-extreme realizable setting, the authors extend inverse gap weighting to selecting k options. They provide a regret guarantee and computation roughly linear in the number of options per step. For millions of options, they introduce a hierarchy that imposes structure on mean rewards. Under this model, the number of relevant options per context is reduced exponentially, replacing the corresponding arm-count dependence in the regret bound with logarithmic dependence.

An implementation using hierarchical linear functions outperforms the evaluated benchmarks in simulated bandit-feedback experiments on extreme multi-label classification datasets. On a dataset with three million options, average inference takes 7.9 milliseconds, a reported hundredfold improvement. The efficiency results rely on exploiting the proposed hierarchy rather than treating every option independently.
icml-2021-top-k-extreme-contextual-bandi.tldr: A structured arm hierarchy makes selecting multiple contextual-bandit actions efficient even in experiments with millions of options.

paragraphs: A collection of pretrained models contains knowledge learned from different large-scale datasets. Applying ordinary transfer learning separately to every model can be expensive and does not fully combine that knowledge. Zoo-Tuning addresses this by learning how to transfer parameters from multiple source models into a model for the target task.

The method first uses a learnable channel alignment layer, then adaptively aggregates the aligned pretrained parameters. Alignment and aggregation jointly support combining source information while adapting it to the downstream problem. The authors report that this adaptive aggregation substantially reduces computation during both training and inference.

A lighter version further reduces inference storage by using a temporal ensemble of batch-average gating values. The approach is evaluated on reinforcement learning, image classification, and facial landmark detection. The reported experiments show more effective and efficient transfer from the model collection. Its contribution is to make the collection itself a source of learnable, combined parameters, rather than treating transfer as a separate exercise for each pretrained model.
icml-2021-zoo-tuning-adaptive-transfer-f.tldr: Zoo-Tuning aligns and adaptively combines pretrained model parameters to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of transfer learning.
